SAA Crash Landing?

By: Sophia Phirippides | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
SAA could be in business rescue, a first time for a State owned enterprise, but how can it avoid insolvency, when the airline is making a loss of over 500 000 rand a minute?

Unique Selling Point:
With bailout after bailout over the years, Is SAA now the victim of a plot to have it sold off or is it indeed a failed enterprise dogged by corruption and over staffing?

After an industrial dispute over pay that was settled with a payment rise in February next year, provided SAA has the money then to afford it, South African Airways has become less about passengers and travel than internal wrangling about where the bailout money went and why the push for privatisation. The blame for SAA’s financial woes is like a tennis match, between procurement corruption on the one hand, and over staffing on the other. Is it time for government to resign itself to privatisation, with the fallout of staff redundancies and the embezzlers of past tender money getting off the hook? Or can the organization be cleaned up under public management to fly the South African flag proudly once more?

Summary:
According to the Solidarity union, fly South African Airways and lose the country cash. How did we get to such a state that grounding all the SAA flights could actually save us money? Or should we listen to NUMSA that claims that the heart of the recent strike was not pay but a response to a deliberate plan to collapse the company to sell, and cover-up corruption... that management threatens workers with their levels of pay and their future employment, when the management are actually responsible for the collapse.
So should the top be cleaned up and refreshed to renegotiate contracts and get the airline back on track? Or should Solidarity’s application for SAA to be placed under business rescue be implemented? But can the country take any view when there is a lack of recent financials coming out of SAA?
The issues have mounted up to culminate in political intrigue and manoeuvring. However, all the while the economy of South Africa is being shattered, with the infighting within SAA and other SOEs at large threatening to bring the country and its people to an economic standstill.

Further information:
We set up the story with a timeline of the main events and issues that have brought South African Airways to this crossroads. Experts and role players will navigate the routes through SAA’s bumpy descent to land at crisis after crisis and provide their ideas on the way forward.


Barbara Curson, SOE expert and researcher, speaks to SAA’s economic failures and gives a timeline of the key events that have impacted the trajectory of the airline.

We get comment from Treasury, from Finance Minister Tito Mboweni, focussing on his earlier comments, that the airline should be closed down.

Phakamile Hlubi-Majola of Numsa, clarifies that the strike negotiations faltered, not because of the wage dispute, but because Numsa demanded that contracts that were bleeding the airline dry needed to be renegotiated in order for the airline to stay afloat and for members to keep their jobs.

Werner Human of Solidarity, a minority union, which has filed a court application to put SAA under business rescue, will elaborate on the business rescue plan, they have devised together with industry experts, of course, this involves bringing in a private equity partner - ultimately leading to the privatisation of the airline – but Human believes that their plan can really rescue SAA and save jobs going forward. They assert that SAA is technically insolvent and is losing over half a million rand a minute.

ROR from SAA themselves and their plan going forward.

The current status with regards to Salaries is that only 50% of monthly salaries will be paid by the 27th of November, and staff have been asked to wait for the other 50% next week, this is in anticipation of a 2 Billion rand operational bailout that the airline has requested from government, the announcement will be made on Monday the 2nd of December. Should the bailout not be forthcoming SAA may be forced to close its doors.


Experts we plan to interview:
Phakamile Hlubi-Majola (NUMSA)

Tito Mboweni, Finance Minister

Werner Human, Solidarity (Union)

Barbara Curson, CA and financial columnist – Money Web

Deon Fredericks, Interim CFO, SAA

Expert:
Ms. Phakamile Hlubi-Majola
Mr. Tito Mboweni
Mr. Werner Human
Mr. Deon Fredericks

Press Release:


A major SAA rescue operation got off the ground this week. With intervention from the President, the board has placed the airline under Business rescue.

Script:


LINK: Fifty seven billion rands is what SAA has cost the South African taxpayer with bailout after bailout over the years. The airline can no longer hide the fact that it is insolvent and jeopardised workers’ salaries.

Phakamile: If SAA is just shut down. That's 11000 jobs that are lost.

Zazi: It's the worst time. And you know I think now employees are really scared for their livelihoods.

VO: November 2019 - the mood at the airline is increasingly uneasy. Its future hangs in the balance. //
21st November - Minority union Solidarity files a court application to put SAA under business rescue, an unprecedented move by a third party.

Werner: Business rescue is an attempt to save a company.

VO: After three years of intensive research Solidarity believed they had a plan to save the airline, according to Deputy CEO Werner He-mun.

Werner: It's a mechanism designed to avoid an inevitable circumstance for a company if they go down a particular road to end up in liquidation And that's the that's a stark reality that the SAA faces.

VO: November 27th, - Solidarity's business rescue application is opposed by the Department of Public enterprises and SAA.

// But only a week later in a shock twist of events, a leaked memo from the president's office instructs cabinet to put SAA under voluntary business rescue, and justifies it as "the only viable route open to government to avoid an uncontrolled implosion".

Werner: The reason why they didn’t go the route of an existing application is simply this - they want to retain control as far as possible on the business rescue proceedings.

VO: December 5th - Government's first nominated Business practitioner, Les Matuson is appointed. Reacting to the appointment, Solidarity, and unions Numsa and SACCA, are up in arms that they are not consulted in the selection process.

Werner: The unions is in a united front to make sure that the practitioner appointed and the process that follows is indeed correctly done and done with the scrutiny of all stakeholders.

LINK: But this crisis didn't happen overnight.

Ryk: The last financial results we've seen was in 2017. The operating loss there 3.6 billion rand. The total debt of the SAA is more than 40 billion. We don't know what the assets are but it's a lot less than that. So it is totally insolvent.

VO: Ryk van Niekerk, editor of Moneyweb, has monitored the ongoing SAA saga closely over the years.

Ryk: There were a few years around 2010 where it did show a profit but since 2011, it was sustained losses.

Devi: So what happened after 2010?

Ryk: Bad management. Definitely.

VO: And this bad management continued with a series of CEO's coming and going, government interference and blatant corruption and looting at the airline.

Ryk: Many airlines around the world have failed and they were relatively well managed. Just imagine if you have all of those factors. It is a recipe for doom.

VO: November 15th - A week long downing of tools by the National Union of Metalworkers of South Africa (Numsa) and the South African Cabin Crew Association (SACCA) reportedly costs the airline over R350 million rands.

// Phakamile Hlubi-Majola National Spokesperson for Numsa is emphatic that the strike action was a last resort.


Phakamile: Long before, we went on the strike, we were informed by the executive management of SAA that there was no money for salaries in November and December.

VO: By the end of November SAA staff are on tenterhooks, according to President of SACCA, Zazi Nsi-banyoni Mu-gambi.

Zazi: There was some sort of communique to the employees even overseas to say be on standby; 4PM there's a big announcement that's gonna be made.
People were loitering the passages, panicking as to what is their future. 4PM came and gone.

VO: Uncertainty reigns - salaries are paid but nobody knows how. Three days later yet another media statement by the Department of Public Enterprises er-tributes the sudden "deterioration of SAA's financial position" to the strike action.

Devi: They are blaming you guys.

Phakamile: We all know that SAA's problems have nothing to do with workers. they have everything to do with the bloated procurement spend, a lot of which has been identified through various forensic reports as being either corrupt or mismanaged. Not one of those reports have been implemented
Werner: As far back as 2017 The auditor general raised the question, why is SAA not placed under business rescue, they ought to have done so.

LINK: The board of SAA has failed to deliver its financials since 2017 which is in effect a breach of the Public Finance Management Act. And the fact that they didn't appear before the Standing Committee on Public Accounts in Parliament makes it difficult for their actions to be seen as transparent.

Devi: What do you read into the fact that SAA hasn't published any financials since 2017.

Ryk: If they do publish it they will be declared insolvent. If it was a commercial entity it would have been liquidated. It contravened so many sections of the companies act for not having done so.

Zazi: Two years without financials and then we are told that the strike is what crippled, you know SAA. I mean take a look. Take a look at your backyard and look if things are OK and it's blatant that it's not OK.

VO: The unions insist that even though they secured a 5.9% wage increase, their greatest victory was the establishment of an empowered task team that would look at ways to reduce costs.

Phakamile: At South African Airways technical for example, we've already saved them 82 million just with having these conversations with management.

VO: But it's SAA's 40 billion Rand debt vacuum that finally brings the situation to a head, when on Monday December the 2nd the DPE announces a "radical restructure" of the national carrier, dependent on funding. But that didn’t last long, because by Wednesday, the funds clearly had not materialised and Business rescue was on the table.

Werner: There's a few consequences if you've initiated these proceedings. There is a moratorium on legal proceedings to be instituted against a company, which is important. Amongst other things, the property that is in current possession of the SAA, even though they might not be the owner of all of that remains intact. The business rescue practitioner may also renegotiate and suspend certain provisions and obligations of the SAA. So this, we would argue, has a stabilizing effect on the entire SAA group as a whole.

VO: Central to SAA's business rescue plan is securing a private equity partner, much like what Solidarity and other role players had been proposing all along.

Werner: There’s a few interesting turnaround stories. Air New Zealand, they were 100 per cent state owned and state controlled . What they found is it simply did not work and they went the Telkom route. They partially privatized I think also 51/ 49 and they are now profitable.

VO: Attempts to get comment from SAA and the DPE proved futile.

Ryk: There is no more money left. The SAA is in such a deep hole. It cannot survive or continue to remain in business without significant interventions

VO: Business rescue is not a silver bullet, but it does put a pause on liquidation. R4 Billion rand in cash and guarantees, from government and the private sector, are a short term lifeline, and with the independent business practitioner at the helm, SAA's future and ownership lies solely in his hands.
Werner: This is most certainly a precedent setting moment although this application has not been in the courts we have now a state owned enterprise that has placed itself in business rescue.

Phakamile: We are literally playing this by the hour. Yeah because it is very difficult to predict exactly how this is going to end.

Is it time for government to resign itself to privatisation, with the fallout of staff redundancies and the embezzlers of past tender money getting off the hook? Or can the organization be cleaned up under public management to fly the South African flag proudly once more?
metadata.Summary: According to the Solidarity union, fly South African Airways and lose the country cash. How did we get to such a state that grounding all the SAA flights could actually save us money? Or should we listen to NUMSA that claims that the heart of the recent strike was not pay but a response to a deliberate plan to collapse the company to sell, and cover-up corruption... that management threatens workers with their levels of pay and their future employment, when the management are actually responsible for the collapse. So should the top be cleaned up and refreshed to renegotiate contracts and get the airline back on track? Or should Solidarity’s application for SAA to be placed under business rescue be implemented? But can the country take any view when there is a lack of recent financials coming out of SAA? The issues have mounted up to culminate in political intrigue and manoeuvring. However, all the while the economy of South Africa is being shattered, with the infighting within SAA and other SOEs at large threatening to bring the country and its people to an economic standstill.
metadata.Further information: We set up the story with a timeline of the main events and issues that have brought South African Airways to this crossroads. Experts and role players will navigate the routes through SAA’s bumpy descent to land at crisis after crisis and provide their ideas on the way forward. Barbara Curson, SOE expert and researcher, speaks to SAA’s economic failures and gives a timeline of the key events that have impacted the trajectory of the airline. We get comment from Treasury, from Finance Minister Tito Mboweni, focussing on his earlier comments, that the airline should be closed down. Phakamile Hlubi-Majola of Numsa, clarifies that the strike negotiations faltered, not because of the wage dispute, but because Numsa demanded that contracts that were bleeding the airline dry needed to be renegotiated in order for the airline to stay afloat and for members to keep their jobs. Werner Human of Solidarity, a minority union, which has filed a court application to put SAA under business rescue, will elaborate on the business rescue plan, they have devised together with industry experts, of course, this involves bringing in a private equity partner - ultimately leading to the privatisation of the airline – but Human believes that their plan can really rescue SAA and save jobs going forward. They assert that SAA is technically insolvent and is losing over half a million rand a minute. ROR from SAA themselves and their plan going forward. The current status with regards to Salaries is that only 50% of monthly salaries will be paid by the 27th of November, and staff have been asked to wait for the other 50% next week, this is in anticipation of a 2 Billion rand operational bailout that the airline has requested from government, the announcement will be made on Monday the 2nd of December. Should the bailout not be forthcoming SAA may be forced to close its doors. Experts we plan to interview: Phakamile Hlubi-Majola (NUMSA) Tito Mboweni, Finance Minister Werner Human, Solidarity (Union) Barbara Curson, CA and financial columnist – Money Web Deon Fredericks, Interim CFO, SAA
